text: So first of all, I'm gonna hit upon some of the key highlights in terms of where we are today. The governor didn't make this decision lightly. Basically, he made this decision last week because of the recent significant spikes, not just in the number of coronavirus cases, but also the related deaths. Also here in Washington state, the projection is for both of those statistics to actually probably hit its peak here in the next couple of weeks. The good news is that most people recognize the seriousness of the virus and are staying at home and of course, practicing social distancing as best as we can. The positive on this is that here in Washington state is that we are seeing a bending or a flattening of the curve and I think as we're all aware, the reason for this is to ensure that our healthcare system does not become overwhelmed. At the same time, the city of Lakewood, we continue to move forward with the implementation of our continuity of operations plan. We continue to operate under a proclamation of emergency and we continue to provide key municipal services. City Hall, police station, senior activity center, our parks, as well as schools, libraries, businesses, a number of nonprofits have all been closed. Unfortunately, a number of meeting and events have either been canceled or postponed. City staff continues to take leadership roles, not just in our own EOC, but also the Pierce County EOC, our joint information committee at the regional level. We've created a COVID-19 webpage and we continue to work with a number of our partners here at the local, state and federal level. Something of interest is tomorrow morning, our economic development director, Becky Newton and our communications manager, Bryn Grimley are gonna send out an email to all the emails, listservs that we have specific to both economic development and city activities in general. And the purpose of that is to send out a link regarding all the business resources that are available for businesses to be able to take advantage of as it relates to the recently adopted CARES Act. So look for that, that'll be going out first thing in the morning. And it's not just for small businesses, it's also for nonprofit organizations and veterans organizations as well. I think as we know, the current recommendation from state and federal government is for people to only leave their home if absolutely necessary. Because again, here in Washington state at least, we're expecting to crest nationally. I think the crest is projected to occur later this month or the early part of May. Some quick numbers, as of yesterday, approximately 350,000 people in the United States have been diagnosed with the virus and over 10,300 have died. The United States is now the world leader in the number of those who have the virus or at least in terms of the numbers that we have. As of yesterday, there were almost 8,000 people in Washington state who have been diagnosed with COVID-19 and 338 have passed away. As of this afternoon here in Pierce County, the number is 717 who have been diagnosed and 12 have passed away. While in Lakewood, there are 59 confirmed cases and we've lost three of our citizens to this virus. At Western State Hospital, the update that we have from earlier this afternoon is actually unchanged from yesterday. There are 18 employees and six patients, including one deceased. What's also interesting is that the age group, originally when this came out, it was basically people 60 and over who were being infected. That is still true in terms of the people who are dying, 60, 65 and over seems to be the majority of those folks. However, in terms of who's being diagnosed, 27% of the cases are between the ages of 20 and 39, 34% are between the ages of 40 and 59 and 26 between the ages of 60 and 79. So fairly evenly distributed across the board there. So this is not a virus that's just impacting one segment of our population. It is significantly impacting most, if not all segments. Those under 19 years old still represent only 2% of the cases. Another issue that we've been dealing with is the governor's directive on what businesses are essential and what businesses are non-essential. In summary, the city of Lakewood, we have taken the position to direct businesses to the governor's portal. The governor has created some guidelines for businesses to consider, to determine whether they're essential or non-essential. And while businesses can and should be able to make that determination, the city of Lakewood is not gonna step in and do that for them. The fact is, is that most businesses are doing what they need to do to get through this. Right now, the city, we're okay on personal protective equipment or PPE. However, we have put in a resupply order in partnership with West Pierce Fire and Rescue for our first responders, particularly in the area of masks. But at this point in time, we're good. So knock on wood, hopefully we'll be able to get a resupply here in the next week or two. The Colobo Park School District has been doing an absolutely phenomenal job on several fronts. They are leading the way other than the Tacoma School District in providing free meals for children in Lakewood and JBLM and the age group of kindergarten through seniors in high school. They also partner with the YMCA early on to create a childcare facility at two of their elementary schools for first responders and healthcare workers. And they're in the process of now beginning to connect online with their students and their parents. And probably more information is expected to come this week is what we understand. And I think as you probably all heard earlier this afternoon, the governor and the OSPI superintendent announced that the school year for this year has essentially been canceled. And so everything that will continue through June will be done in a different way. Pierce Transit has significantly cut back on their bus service. Ridership is down almost 60%. Could even have decreased from, those were numbers from last week. The Pierce County Library has been closed for well over a month now. And they're in the process of trying to order some more online books and online video, given that the demand for that has been pretty, pretty significant. WSDOT has made the decision in partnership with the governor to essentially suspend the majority of their state highway projects. Also earlier this week, Sound Transit made the decision to do the same thing. SSMCP of which Lakewood is a part of, we sent a letter to the governor a couple of weeks ago, asking the governor not to do that since traffic has been really low and it's a good time to do this work. We did not receive a response back to that other than suspension of WSDOT projects will continue for the foreseeable future. Early on, one of the programs that the city suspended was our rental housing safety inspection program, given the personal interaction there. However, last week, our team, and I really wanna call out our administrative assistant, Heather Hallstrott, for coming up with a way to actually do it via video and pictures. And so that program is up and running and actually the landlords, the feedback has been very positive because a lot of people have a lot of time in their hands right now. And so they wanna get those inspections out of the way. A number of meetings and events have either been canceled or postponed. We're in the process right now of evaluating all city events through the end of July, which would include Summerfest. Actually, we heard from the Lakewood Sister Cities Association that it's unlikely that our sister city delegation will travel over here in July from Gimhae Republic of South Korea as they did last year. So just like we had to postpone the youth summit, we had to postpone and push off the night farmer's market. There's probably a number of other events that we're either gonna have to cancel outright or postpone to later on in the year. And we hope to have an update for you in the next week or two. As you know, legislative bodies could meet. And again, the guidance provided by the governor is that your agenda should be necessary and routine. And as we look at your upcoming agendas, we have moved a couple of items, generally speaking, they do meet either one or the other or both and that's okay. However, if the council, if you wish to make changes there, it's your agenda and you're certainly free to do that. But what we're trying to do is we're trying to stay on task. For example, human services, that's a process that kicks off later this summer. And we don't wanna deviate from that given that upcoming funding, that funding cycle. On the police side, at the request of the jails we're testing the temperature of prisoners before they go to jails, but at the same time, both the Nisqually Jail and the Pierce County Jail has been generally speaking, not accepting new customers, if you will. And so a lot of work that we've been doing out there has been site and release. At the same time, calls for service across the board are down from a year ago. Domestic violence issues seem to go up and down, but overall they're about the same or a little bit lower on a year to date comparison for that time period as well. One of the things that Chief Zara was gonna do on this Wednesday, given that typically Wednesdays is a day that we have overlap for training with a number of our commission law enforcement officers. And he's gonna use that to do a bit of a bike emphasis out into our commercial areas as well as some of our neighborhoods given some of the nonsense that has recently picked up there. Our senior activity center is closed. However, our senior center staff have created and initiated a phone tree to check on our older adults to make sure that they're okay during this time of crisis. Last week, the president and Congress, and this week they continue to have discussions about another stimulus package and looking to include infrastructure projects in that. And they need to be shovel ready. This morning, our team, we got together to talk about that. And some of the projects that certainly will be shovel ready on the roadside would be the JBLM North Project, North Access Project, as well as Stillicum Boulevard from Weller all the way down to Far West. However, there could be others such as Nianza or 112th and Lakewood Drive from 100th to South Tacoma Way. So as more information becomes available on that, I might be coming back to you and asking you for money to kickstart some design on some of those projects. On the park side, there's a couple of projects at Fort Stillicum Park that we could turn around and have shovel ready pretty quickly. One is redoing the parking lot in the front area of the park, as well as replacing our fuel system down there, which needs to be done. And then the second one would be moving forward with some significant improvements at American Lake Park based on the master plan that is moving forward there. So those are a couple of areas on the park side, not sure if Congress is thinking about parks, but we are in case something does come about. Congress also passed the Families First Coronavirus Response Act. In summary, our human resources and legal team took a look at that and created a policy to make sure that we are in compliance of that. On the finance side, our finance team is beginning and actually working with our emergency services director, John Unfried, our assistant police chief, and getting together the costs that we have incurred so that we can provide a reimbursement submittal to FEMA. This is important based on the president's declaration of an emergency on Friday, March 13. So that is something that we're doing. And when that call comes, we will be ready. At the same time, the city is eligible for $134,000 grant from the federal government under the CARES Act. And it's a particular grant program that provides funding to assist local municipalities and others in preventing, preparing, and responding to the coronavirus, such things such as PPE I talked about a little bit ago, overtime, other equipment, supplies, some training, things along those lines. So between finance and the police department, they're currently working on that. We have until May 29th to submit that. We hope to be able to get that done sooner rather than later. As we look into the future, we are beginning to focus on our recovery and what that looks like, particularly as it relates to our city's finances. I just wanna say three things to start off with. First, we're not gonna jump into any conclusions without having some kind of an understanding of what the impact is, which means having some kind of empirical data showing what the trends are. We know it's gonna be bad, but again, we're not gonna jump to conclusions. That's not gonna get us anywhere. Secondly, we're not gonna panic, because again, that doesn't help. And then third, I'd just like to point out, we have very excellent financial policies in how we have developed our budgets in the past, and that will help us through this process, including as it relates to 2020. Actually, I'm not all, I mean, I'm concerned about 2020, but the fact is, is that we have reserves in place, our strategic reserve, for example, to address situations like this. Really, the challenge is gonna be as we look out into the next biennium, and at the end of the day, it's gonna come down to math. But hopefully, the federal government is gonna step up, and we've been in close communication with both our congressmen, as well as the offices of our two senators, that the next CARES Act includes backfill funding for loss of discretionary tax revenues that cities are gonna be experiencing, and we have been getting positive feedback on that. In addition, I've been reaching out to a number of my colleagues in other cities, and asking them to do the same thing. The other thing to remember is that, the current economic recession that we're either in or about to enter, and how bad it's gonna be, and things along those lines, this is a little different. It was not created by bad economic fundamentals. The fact is, is that the economic fundamentals of our nation's economy, as well as our region's economy, was very, very, very strong. This pandemic flu essentially kind of sidetracked that. So, I think at the end of the day, we have a good solid foundation from which to begin on, and which to recover. In addition, the $2.2 trillion CARES Act represents 10% of our country's total GDP, which is absolutely enormous. And it's likely that there's more to come as well. Now, of course, that adds to the deficit, but certainly in the short term, that will help get things back on track. And because of that, we're looking at developing really three financial scenarios. And again, we'll make some good underlying assumptions as best as we can. Really, the first scenario will be, things will be really, really bad in 2020. Actually, that's the same for all three scenarios. But then there'll be a recovery. What does that look like with a recovery beginning in the second half of 2021? The second scenario will be, things will be really bad in 2020, as well as 2021 and recover in 2022. And then the third scenario will be, things will be really, really bad for the next two to three years. And then things really won't be able to pick up until 2023. I think that latter option is, I think the chances or probability of having that happen are probably five to 10%. I think the second scenario, I think you're looking at maybe a 15 to 20%. And I think probably a 50 to 60% chance is what's gonna happen once this thing begins to come back after we come through this whole virus thing. So I wanted to point that out, and we hope to have some information that we can share with you, at least in draft format by the end of this month, if not early, early May. So just again, shows an example of the tremendous relationship and partnership that we have with JBLM. The Stillicum Boulevard Project from Custer to Weller, that was supposed to kick off last week. However, the contractor and their employees, they weren't quite ready. And so right now they're looking at kicking off on Wednesday at this point in time, knock on wood. The Onyx Dry Project, they're also expected to kick off later this week as well. And then the Veterans Dry Project, the bids came in, actually very healthy bids. We got 10 bidders submitted bids, 10 construction companies, five were above, five were below the engineer's estimate. The low bid was from Miles Construction who we've done a lot of work with. And it was like a quarter of a million dollars below the engineer's estimate. And that includes going all the way to the VA as well as doing the parking lot at American Lake Park. As you might remember from Mr. Buschitz telling you that it was likely that we might have to go back and take the savings from Onyx to balance this project out. Well, guess what? No, both projects are gonna have savings. So that's real positive at this point in time. We are checking to make sure that Miles is not just the lowest bidder, but the most responsive bidder as well. And if so, we will have for you as part of your next regular meeting on April 20th, an opportunity for you to consider and award that contract. Something that has come up in our contracts and there's boilerplate language in all of these contracts. And it's certainly in the 30 years I've been doing this, I've written a lot of contracts myself and you always kind of do the stick and paste on something called force majeure. And that's language that's existed for decades. And what it means is that either party, either the city or the contractor doesn't have to be held to the terms of the contractor because of generally speaking acts of God or things like that. Does the pandemic meet that? Yeah, probably so. Now at this point in time, we're not aware of any contractors or even the city looking to have to exercise that. But I just wanted to give you a courtesy heads up that that's out there. speaker: donanderson
text: Yeah, what has happened a couple of things.
